newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 24.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Thursday:
* IBM posted better-than-expected revenues and earnings per share in the first quarter, although earnings were roughly flat.
* The Dow Jones Industrial average finished down 20.87 points at 6,812.72, declining slightly after recording its second-largest point gain ever on Tuesday.
* Walt Disney reported earnings that were stronger than anticipated, helped by higher theme park attendance, films and "Bambi" video sales.
* Faced with declining profits in its sunglasses, contact lenses and lens care businesses, Bausch & Lomb announced plans to cut about 14 percent of its workforce, or 1,900 jobs.
* US Airways announced a return to profitability in the first quarter and its stock rose 18 percent.
* Boeing, battling rival Airbus for the world's fastest-growing commercial aircraft market, is looking to sell 100 aircraft to China.
* Mobil and Chevron posted strong earnings, as did DuPont's Conoco unit. But Phillips Petroleum earnings came in below forecast.
* Saks stock slid following the company's announcement that its first quarter earnings would be well below Wall Street expectations.
* The International Monetary Fund said worldwide economic growth would accelerate again this year to 4.4 percent, but most regions face risks that could affect their outlooks.
* European electronics companies Philips Electronics and Siemens posted earnings gains.
* General Motors workers at a Pontiac, Michigan plant went on strike.
* Market Place: The Toronto Stock Exchange shut its trading floor and moved entirely to computers in order to guard market share and cut costs.
* Midwestern real-estate firms LaSalle Partners and Galbreath plan to merge. Both have significant operations in New York.
* The U.S. Energy Department announced that refrigerators sold in 2001 will have to use 30 percent less electricity than those now on the market.
* Hewlett-Packard said it agreed to buy VeriFone, which makes credit card authorization devices in a $1.15 billion stock swap.

* Quaker Oats said chairman and chief executive William Smithburg, who led the company during its troubled acquisition of the Snapple drinks business, would resign as soon as a successor could be chosen.
* A growing number of U.S. cities not previously known for their cultural attractions, like Orlando, Fla., are trying to lure tourists by promoting cultural events.
